topics.reason: The final nominal attribute clause answers a condition but states an abiding reality.

words.gloss_range: accusative divine name as subject of the emphatic closing clause
words.prose: {{ar:ٱللَّهَ}} ({{tr:allāha}}) returns the divine name in a new case and role. Earlier the name was genitive as the target of gratitude; here it is accusative under the emphatic particle and anchors the two closing predicates. The repetition makes the shift visible: gratitude is owed to God, but God's status does not depend on gratitude. The worship-centered pressure of the name is routed into the attribute seal rather than into another human-action clause.
words.root_gloss_range: unique divine name with worship and disputed bewilderment derivation pressure; locally the subject of the closing attributes

topics.headline: divine name anchors both attributes
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the closing attributes attach explicitly to God, not to an implied or ambiguous subject.
topics.reason: The divine name is the accusative subject governed by the emphatic particle and is followed by two predicates.

topics.headline: same name, changed case and role
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks the ayah's argument through case: from God as target of gratitude to God as subject of independence.
topics.reason: The earlier divine name is genitive under the gratitude preposition, while this occurrence is accusative under the emphatic particle.

topics.headline: name routed into attribute seal
topics.reader_payoff: The reader keeps worship-centered divine-name pressure in view as it is routed into the closing attribute field.
topics.reason: The root pressure colors the proper name, while the local syntax makes it the subject of the self-sufficiency and praise predicates.

words.gloss_range: first qualitative predicate: self-sufficient, free of need
words.prose: {{ar:غَنِىٌّ}} ({{tr:ghaniyyun}}) is the first closing predicate and answers the ingratitude condition with needlessness. The {{ar:غ ن ي}} ({{tr:gh-n-y}}) range can include wealth and enrichment, but this context selects freedom from need: human denial cannot diminish God. Its qualitative pattern and indefinite predicate form present that sufficiency as an abiding attribute, and the same attribute pair returns in definite form at 31:26.
words.root_gloss_range: needlessness, sufficiency, enriching, availing, and wealth; locally divine independence from human gratitude or ingratitude

topics.headline: self-sufficiency nullifies harm
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that ingratitude is answered by God's freedom from need, so denial cannot harm or diminish Him.
topics.reason: The adjective follows the ingratitude condition and selects divine needlessness rather than mere wealth.

topics.headline: stable attribute, not event
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees self-sufficiency stated as a standing quality, not as a reaction produced by human behavior.
topics.reason: The word is nominative as the first predicate and has qualitative adjective form with indefinite predicate marking.

topics.headline: first half of recurring attribute pair
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the closing pair as a surah-local anchor that will return in definite form at 31:26.
topics.reason: The same self-sufficiency and praise pair recurs later in the surah and is tied to denial contexts.

topics.headline: enrichment range narrowed to independence
topics.reader_payoff: The reader retains the richness of the sufficiency family while the local clause selects absolute independence.
topics.reason: The broader root range includes enrichment and sufficiency, but the ingratitude context chooses needlessness as the operative sense.

words.gloss_range: second qualitative predicate: intrinsically praiseworthy
words.prose: {{ar:حَمِيدٌ}} ({{tr:ḥamīdun}}) completes the closing attribute seal. Its {{ar:ح م د}} ({{tr:ḥ-m-d}}) field differs from gratitude: praise concerns inherent excellence, so God remains praiseworthy even if a human covers over benefit. The qualitative form and paired ending with {{ar:غَنِىٌّ}} ({{tr:ghaniyyun}}) bind needlessness and praiseworthiness into the ayah's final answer. The pair also recurs where human rejection cannot alter divine status (14:8; 22:64; 60:6), and it returns in this surah at 31:26.
words.root_gloss_range: praise for inherent excellence, praiseworthiness, and praise-giving; locally intrinsic praiseworthiness independent of human gratitude

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: self-sufficient as the first member of the closing predicate pair

topics.headline: second predicate completes the seal
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the ayah lands on a two-attribute seal, not merely on denial's failure.
topics.reason: The word is nominative as a second predicate after the self-sufficiency predicate and ends the ayah.

topics.headline: praise independent of human gratitude
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that praiseworthiness belongs to God intrinsically and is not created by human acts of gratitude.
topics.reason: The root distinction between praise and gratitude survives, while the local predicate after self-sufficiency selects intrinsic praiseworthiness as the main force.

topics.headline: recurring pair answers rejection
topics.reader_payoff: The reader recognizes the attribute pair as a recurring formula in contexts where human rejection cannot alter divine status.
topics.reason: The attribute pair recurs at 14:8, 22:64, 60:6, and again in the same surah at 31:26.

topics.headline: cadence closes the moral circuit
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the paired predicate endings bind the final semantics: human benefit returns inward, while divine praise remains intact.
topics.reason: The matched indefinite predicate forms and final cadence join the two attributes into a terminal assertion.
